title: Propagation of Chaos in Contextual Flow Maps

paper.title: Propagation of Chaos in Contextual Flow Maps
paper.abstract:
Abstract. We develop a quantitative statistical theory of transformers in the
large-context regime by adopting the abstraction of contextual flow maps (CFMs):
dynamical systems that evolve a distinguished token in the presence of a
contextual measure across a stack of attention blocks. Within this framework,
the finite-context model approximates an idealized infinite-context system in
which the contextual measure is replaced by its underlying population, so that
the context length n n becomes a statistical resource. Exploiting the
McKean–Vlasov structure of the dynamics and the classical machinery of
propagation of chaos, we establish a forward bound controlling the
deviation between the finite- and infinite-context CFMs uniformly along
depth, and a backward bound controlling the deviation between the
corresponding training trajectories uniformly across iterations of online
gradient descent. Both bounds achieve the optimal Wasserstein rate n − 1 / d n^{-1/d} for general CFMs and parametric rate n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} for a restricted class of CFMs that includes transformers as a special case. The analysis rests on a new Eulerian
adjoint formulation of the loss gradient and stability
estimates for the resulting forward–adjoint system, both of which may be of
independent interest.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The transformer architecture, introduced by Vaswani et al. [ 59 ] , is the foundation of modern machine learning systems, from large language models [ 29 ] to Vision Transformers [ 30 ] . A convenient way to view inputs to these models is through a distinguished token x ∈ ℝ d x\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that is updated in the presence of a context of n n tokens z ( 1 ) , … , z ( n ) ∈ ℝ d z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(n)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} encoded by the contextual measure μ = 1 n ​ ∑ i δ z ( i ) \mu= rac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\delta_{z^{(i)}} . In encoder-style models, x x is typically a prepended special token such as [CLS] ; in decoder-style models, it is the current final token whose representation is used to predict the next one. After passing through a deep stack of attention blocks, the model returns an output token y y whose value depends on both x x and its context. We refer to such maps as contextual maps . This viewpoint on transformers was developed in [ 33 ] , where transformers were shown to have universal approximation properties within the class of contextual maps. At the same time, the compositional structure of transformers, like that of deep neural networks more broadly, can be interpreted as a dynamical system, with the network realizing an input-to-output flow map [ 31 , 44 , 22 ] . Combining these perspectives suggests a natural abstraction: transformers as contextual flow maps , namely dynamical systems that evolve an input token-context pair ( x 0 , μ 0 ) (x_{0},\mu_{0}) across layers and produce an output token x 1 x_{1} . We consider a class of general contextual flow maps ( x 0 , μ 0 ) ↦ x 1 (x_{0},\mu_{0})\mapsto x_{1} that include transformers and take the form (1.1a) x ˙ s = 𝒱 ⁡ ( x s , μ s , θ ⁡ ( s ) ) , s ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , \displaystyle\dot{x}_{s}=\mathcal{V}(x_{s},\mu_{s};	heta(s)),\quad s\in[0,1], (1.1b) ∂ s μ s + ∇ ⋅ ( μ s ​ 𝒱 ​ ( ⋅ , μ s , θ ⁡ ( s ) ) ) = 0 , s ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , \displaystyle\partial_{s}\mu_{s}+

Three formalizations of transformers. The contextual measure μ 0 = 1 n ​ ∑ i δ z ( i ) \mu_{0}= rac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\delta_{z^{(i)}} can be regarded as an n n -sample empirical estimator of an underlying population measure μ 0 ∞ \mu_{0}^{\infty} . The contextual flow map ( 1.1 ) then takes this empirical measure as input and produces an output x 1 x_{1} that approximates an idealized infinite-context system, obtained by replacing μ 0 \mu_{0} with μ 0 ∞ \mu_{0}^{\infty} in ( 1.1 ). The infinite-context system is a natural reference because an ideal transformer should be able to operate on arbitrarily long context: as the context grows, the contextual measure μ 0 \mu_{0} resolves the underlying population μ 0 ∞ \mu_{0}^{\infty} ever more faithfully, and a model that fully exploits its context should reflect this in its output. The infinite-context system is exactly the object that does so, and the finite-context model should be understood as approximating it. From this perspective, the context length n n plays the role of a statistical resource: it is the budget the model is given to estimate the population on which the ideal transformer would act. We are thus led to the central question of the paper: How accurately does a finite-context contextual flow map approximate its infinite-context limit, as a function of the context length n n , both at inference time (forward pass) and during training (backward pass)? This question is of practical as well as theoretical interest: although recent advances have substantially extended the usable context window of large language models [ 56 ] , long contexts remain constrained by computational costs, which in turn limit the emergence of new capabilities. Quantifying the dependence on n n therefore informs how aggressively context can be reduced without compromising fidelity to the infinite-context reference. The McKean–Vlasov structure of ( 1.1 ) makes it tractable through the classical machinery of propagation of chaos [ 46 , 55 , 20 , 21 ] . Related work. The input-output behavior of transformers can be formalized in at least three ways: as a sequence-to-sequence map, a measure-to-measure map, and a contextual map; see Figure 1 . The sequence-to-sequence viewpoint models a transformer T : ( ℝ d ) n → ( ℝ d ) n T:(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}	o(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n} as a map from n n input tokens ( x 1 , … , x n ) (x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) to n n output tokens ( y 1 , … , y n ) (y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}) . This early and direct formalization was used to establish approximation results in [ 64 , 1 ] , albeit with architectures whose size grows exponentially in n n . Although this dependence can be alleviated by allowing the embedding dimension to scale with n n , the resulting growth in complexity remains restrictive in modern large-context applications. Early measure-theoretic foundations for attention were developed in [ 60 ] , which interpreted self-attention as a system of self-interacting particles and established regularity properties such as Lipschitz continuity under suitable assumptions. This line of work was substantially extended in the seminal paper [ 54 ] , where transformers were analyzed as a mean-field interacting particle system implementing a measure-to-measure map. This perspective has enabled the use of powerful tools from partial differential equations and Wasserstein gradient flows; see [ 37 , 36 , 13 , 12 , 23 , 17 , 53 , 11 , 24 , 39 , 3 , 2 ] . From a statistical viewpoint, a closely related recent contribution is [ 47 ] , which studies transformers as measure-theoretic associative memory and establishes generalization guarantees together with a matching minimax lower bound under spectral assumptions. Despite its usefulness, however, the measure-to-measure viewpoint does not explicitly capture the central role of the distinguished token. This limitation is addressed by the contextual-map formulation introduced in the [ 33 ] , which established universal approximation within the class of contextual flow maps using architectures whose size is independent of the context length. The relevance of this contextual framework extends well beyond approximation theory. It provides a natural language for the rapidly growing literature on in-context learning with transformers [ 10 , 63 , 35 , 4 , 61 , 26 , 5 ] . Moreover, it captures the structure of settings in which transformers are explicitly deployed as contextual velocity fields , notably in diffusion models [ 51 ] and measure-to-measure regression [ 58 ] . The present work adopts the same contextual viewpoint, but focuses on statistical questions rather than expressivity alone. The statistical behavior of transformers as the context length grows has received relatively little attention. Recent works [ 9 , 7 ] study the convergence of a single attention head applied to n n i.i.d. tokens to its infinite-token limit. While both establish a parametric n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} rate of convergence, the latter draws a more subtle picture near the hardmax limit. Our contribution differs in two major ways. First, we study a deep stack of attention layers using contextual flow maps rather than a single attention layer. In a deep stack the context tokens interact through the shared velocity field 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , so they lose their initial independence after the first layer; bounding the deviation from the infinite-context limit therefore requires tracking the growth of correlations across layers. Second, we also study the generalization of training dynamics from finite to infinite context length. Our analysis is accordingly closer in spirit to the theory of propagation of chaos for McKean–Vlasov dynamics. We emphasize that in our setting the term refers to quantitative mean-field stability bounds rather than the convergence of finite marginals to product measures as in [ 49 ] . Nevertheless, we adopt it as it has become standard in the machine learning literature [ 27 , 50 , 41 , 42 , 40 , 28 , 19 ] . While our work does not require the full apparatus of the theory, we borrow its key structural insight: controlling deviations through regularity of the velocity fields, in both the forward and the backward pass. Uniform-in-time propagation of chaos for the backward pass of two-layer feedforward networks—simple maps f θ : ℝ d → ℝ d f_{	heta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}	o\mathbb{R}^{d} —was recently established in [ 43 ] . We extend these results to contextual flow maps, which (i) account for depth and (ii) depend on an evolving measure. Our contributions. We initiate a quantitative statistical theory of contextual flow maps in the large-context regime, treating the context length n n as the central statistical resource. Under mild regularity assumptions on the velocity field 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , our main results are the following. (C1) Forward propagation of chaos. We establish a quantitative deviation bound between the finite-context contextual flow map ( 1.1 ) and its infinite-context limit, holding uniformly along the depth of the network (Theorem 2.1 ). The analysis explicitly tracks the propagation of correlations introduced at each layer by the shared velocity field—a mechanism that is absent from the single-layer analyses of [ 9 , 7 ] . (C2) Backward propagation of chaos. We obtain a deviation bound between the Online Gradient Descent (OGD) training trajectory of a finite-context model and that of its infinite-context counterpart, holding uniformly over all iterations of the algorithm (Theorem 2.2 ). This extends the recent two-layer feedforward result of [ 43 ] along two structural axes: (i) depth, through a stack of attention layers with parameters shared across tokens, and (ii) interaction with an evolving contextual measure that is itself transported across layers. (C3) Adjoint equation for contextual flows. We derive an Eulerian adjoint formulation of the loss gradient (Theorem 3.1 in Section 3 ) that couples a covector adjoint for the distinguished token to a scalar adjoint test function for the contextual measure. This formulation underlies all of our stability analysis and extends naturally to the Riemannian setting relevant to post-LayerNorm transformers. (C4) Stability estimates. Our results rest on a new set of stability estimates for the contextual flow and the loss gradient (Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 in Section 4 ), established uniformly in depth and uniformly along the parameter path. We further show in Section 4.3 that the standard transformer architecture—both self-attention and MLP layers—satisfies these estimates with Lipschitz constants that are independent of the embedding dimension and parameter count , suggesting a structural reason why transformers train stably across model scales. Assumptions. Our results rest on two sets of assumptions, stated as Assumptions 5.1 and 5.2 . The first is purely technical: routine regularity conditions (compactness, smoothness of the various objects entering the definition of CFMs) of the kind required by any analysis of this type. Some can likely be relaxed, but regularity of some form is unavoidable. The second assumption plays a more substantive role. It is not needed to establish our slow rates n − 1 / d n^{-1/d} ; rather, it is the precise structural ingredient that upgrades these to the parametric rate n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} . It posits that the velocity field 𝒱 \mathcal{V} driving the CFM ( 1.1 ) takes the form 𝒱 ⁡ ( x , μ , θ ) = ℱ ⁡ ( ∫ ℝ d F ⁡ ( x , y , θ ) ​ 𝑑 μ ​ ( y ) ) + G ⁡ ( x , θ ) . \mathcal{V}(x,\mu;	heta)=\mathcal{F}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}F(x,y;	heta)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(y)ight)+G(x;	heta). for sufficiently regular functions ℱ , F \mathcal{F},F and G G , so that μ \mu is applied linearly . Crucially, this is precisely the structure of self-attention ( 1.2 ) with a multi-layer perceptron (MLP): the transformer-based CFMs that motivate this work satisfy Assumption 5.2 by construction , and therefore enjoy the fast parametric rate. sections.heading: 2. Main results
sections.text: We work throughout with the contextual flow map ( 1.1 ), which sends an input pair ( x 0 , μ 0 ) ∈ ℝ d × 𝒫 ⁡ ( ℝ d ) (x_{0},\mu_{0})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) together with a parameter path θ : [ 0 , 1 ] → ℝ p \theta:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^{p} to the output token x 1 = x 1 ​ ( x 0 , μ 0 , θ ) ∈ ℝ d x_{1}=x_{1}(x_{0},\mu_{0};\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . All results below are stated for the inputs and the velocity field 𝒱 \mathcal{V} : (i) under the standard regularity hypotheses collected in Assumption 5.1 ; or (ii) under the special form of 𝒱 \mathcal{V} specified in Assumption 5.2 . We verify in Appendix E that both assumptions are met by the self-attention vector field ( 1.2 ) and standard MLP layers with dimension-free constants. We let 𝐀 \mathbf{A} denote the bundle of constants appearing in the assumptions, and write C = C ⁡ ( 𝐀 ) C=C(\mathbf{A}) for any positive constant depending only on these parameters (in particular, independent of p p , d d , and n n ).

Because the dependence of x 1 x_{1} on the entire path θ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \theta(\cdot) is mediated implicitly through the coupled token–measure system ( 1.1 ), computing the Fréchet derivative δ ​ ℒ / δ ​ θ \delta\mathcal{L}/\delta\theta is non-trivial; an explicit Eulerian-adjoint formula is derived in Appendix B and underlies the regularity analysis below. In Theorem 2.2 below, we establish two results: one for λ \lambda small (or zero) and one for λ \lambda large. The latter yields stability across all iterations of online gradient descent.

sections.heading: Online gradient descent.
sections.text: We train the model by online gradient descent (OGD) 1 1 1 OGD reduces to Stochastic Gradient Descent if we further assume that the samples are i.i.d. on a stream of samples. At each iteration k ∈ ℕ k\in\mathbb{N} , the parameter path is updated using a triple of observations ( x 0 k , μ 0 k , y 0 k ) (x_{0}^{k},\mu_{0}^{k},y_{0}^{k}) according to (2.3) θ k + 1 ​ ( s ) = ( 1 − η ​ λ ) ​ θ k ​ ( s ) − η ​ δ ​ ℒ ​ ( θ k , μ 0 k , x 0 k , y 0 k ) δ ​ θ ​ ( s ) , s ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , \theta_{k+1}(s)\;=\;(1-\eta\lambda)\,\theta_{k}(s)\;-\;\eta\,\frac{\delta\mathcal{L}(\theta_{k};\mu_{0}^{k},x_{0}^{k},y_{0}^{k})}{\delta\theta}(s),\qquad s\in[0,1], where η > 0 \eta>0 is a fixed step size and λ ∈ [ 0 , η − 1 ) \lambda\in[0,\eta^{-1}) . OGD is a faithful idealization of how large transformers are pretrained: a (close to) single pass over an enormous corpus, in which each step sees a new batch that need not be independent of other observations.

sections.heading: 2.1. Propagation of chaos for the forward pass
sections.text: We first analyze the inference-time behavior. Fix a parameter path θ \theta , a distinguished token x 0 ∈ ℝ d x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , and a contextual measure μ 0 ∈ 𝒫 ⁡ ( ℝ d ) \mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) , and let z ( 1 ) , … , z ( n ) ∼ iid μ 0 z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(n)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\mu_{0} . We compare the contextual flow driven by the population context μ 0 \mu_{0} to the one driven by the empirical context (2.4) μ ^ 0 ≔ 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n δ z ( i ) , \widehat{\mu}_{0}\;\coloneqq\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{z^{(i)}}, denoting the corresponding solutions of ( 1.1 ) by ( x s , μ s ) (x_{s},\mu_{s}) and ( x ^ s , μ ^ s ) (\widehat{x}_{s},\widehat{\mu}_{s}) . The central point is that the bound below is uniform in the depth variable s ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] s\in[0,1] , including at output time s = 1 s=1 . Such a result is non-trivial since after the first layer the n n context tokens are no longer independent: they are coupled through the shared velocity field 𝒱 \mathcal{V} . Controlling the build-up of correlations across layers is precisely what propagation-of-chaos arguments are designed for in the McKean–Vlasov literature [ 55 , 20 ] , and it is what we adapt here to the contextual setting. The proof of the next theorem uses a standard Grönwall bound. It does not suffer from a classical exponential deterioration since we assume s ≤ 1 s\leq 1 . Theorem 2.1 (Forward propagation of chaos) . Adopt Assumption 5.1 and suppose that d ≥ 3 d\geq 3 . There exists a constant C = C ⁡ ( 𝐀 ) C=C(\mathbf{A}) such that, with probability at least 1 − 4 ​ exp ⁡ ( − n 1 − 2 / d ) 1-4\exp\!\left(-n^{\,1-2/d}\right) , (2.5) sup s ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] W 1 ( μ s , μ ^ s ) ≤ C n − 1 / d and sup s ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] | x s − x ^ s | ≤ C n − 1 / d . \sup_{s\in[0,1]}\mathrm{W}_{1}\!\left(\mu_{s},\widehat{\mu}_{s}\right)\;\leq\;C\,n^{-1/d}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\,\bigl|x_{s}-\widehat{x}_{s}\bigr|\;\leq\;C\,n^{-1/d}. If 𝒱 \mathcal{V} additionally satisfies Assumption 5.2 , then for every δ ∈ ( 0 , 1 / 2 ) \delta\in(0,1/2) , (2.6) sup s ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] | x s − x ^ s | ≤ C ​ log ⁡ ( δ − 1 ) n , \sup_{s\in[0,1]}\,\bigl|x_{s}-\widehat{x}_{s}\bigr|\;\leq\;C\,\sqrt{\frac{\log(\delta^{-1})}{n}}, with probability at least 1 − δ 1-\delta . A few comments are in order. First regarding the slow rate ( 2.5 ): Without further structural assumptions on the CFM such as Assumption 5.2 , the rate n − 1 / d n^{-1/d} is the best one can hope for already at the level of the input contextual measure, by the Wasserstein law of large numbers [ 25 , Ch. 2] : the contextual flow therefore does not amplify the empirical noise, and the finite-context output is statistically as good as the input it consumes. When μ 0 \mu_{0} is supported on a submanifold of intrinsic dimension d ′ < d d^{\prime}<d , the same bound holds with n − 1 / d n^{-1/d} replaced by n − 1 / d ′ n^{-1/d^{\prime}} [ 62 ] ; this is the practically relevant regime in transformer pretraining, where token embeddings are believed to concentrate on a low-dimensional manifold despite the ambient dimension d d being in the hundreds or thousands. The condition d ≥ 3 d\geq 3 is purely cosmetic: the more general Theorem A.2 in Appendix A holds for every d ≥ 1 d\geq 1 , with the rate n − 1 / d n^{-1/d} adjusted according to the Wasserstein law of large numbers. More generally, these bounds instantiate a pattern recently articulated by Raginsky and Recht [ 52 ] : the deterministic core of the result is a Wasserstein-stability statement for the flow, into which the data assumption is plugged ex post via a Wasserstein law of large numbers, separating the geometry of the dynamics from the probabilistic assumptions on the data. The fast/parametric rate ( 2.6 ) is quite striking: despite the presence of multiple layers that compromise independent, the parametric rate persists thanks to propagation of chaos across layers for structured CFMs such as transformers. Details are provided in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 2.2. Propagation of chaos along online gradient descent
sections.text: We now turn to the corresponding question on the backward pass, which is significantly more delicate. Let { ( x 0 k , μ 0 k , y 0 k ) } k ∈ ℕ \{(x_{0}^{k},\mu_{0}^{k},y_{0}^{k})\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}} be the population (infinite context) data stream and, at each step k k , form the empirical contextual measure (2.7) μ ^ 0 k ≔ 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n δ z ( k , i ) , z ( k , 1 ) , … , z ( k , n ) ∼ iid μ 0 k . \widehat{\mu}_{0}^{\,k}\;\coloneqq\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{z^{(k,i)}},\qquad z^{(k,1)},\ldots,z^{(k,n)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\mu_{0}^{k}. Starting both trajectories from the same path θ 0 \theta_{0} , we compare the two OGD trajectories produced by ( 2.3 ): the population OGD { θ k } k ∈ ℕ \{\theta_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}} driven by ( x 0 k , μ 0 k , y 0 k ) (x_{0}^{k},\mu_{0}^{k},y_{0}^{k}) , and the empirical OGD { θ ^ k } k ∈ ℕ \{\widehat{\theta}_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}} driven by ( x 0 k , μ ^ 0 k , y 0 k ) (x_{0}^{k},\widehat{\mu}_{0}^{\,k},y_{0}^{k}) with θ ^ 0 = θ 0 \widehat{\theta}_{0}=\theta_{0} . The statistical quantity of interest is the deviation ‖ θ k − θ ^ k ‖ L ∞ \|\theta_{k}-\widehat{\theta}_{k}\|_{L^{\infty}} . The behavior of this deviation depends on the regularization parameter λ \lambda . Without enough regularization, parameter trajectories may drift apart after a large number of iterations and the deviation can in principle accumulate; strong enough regularization, by contrast, contracts the dynamics at every step and yields a bound that is uniform in the number of training iterations. The proofs are provided in Appendix C and Appendix D . Also, three features of this result are worth emphasizing. Rate. Both bounds ( 2.8 ),( 2.10 ) match the inference-time rate n − 1 / d n^{-1/d} of Theorem 2.1 (sharpening to n − 1 / d ′ n^{-1/d^{\prime}} on a d ′ d^{\prime} -dimensional submanifold) and n 1 / 2 n^{1/2} under Assumption 5.2 : training incurs no statistical loss beyond, even though the OGD iterates depend on the full history of empirical samples and gradients. Role of regularization. The dichotomy between (i) and (ii) is genuine. Statement (i) is unconditional but limited to a horizon k ≲ 1 / η k\lesssim 1/\eta , beyond which Grönwall bounds deteriorate exponentially; statement (ii) trades this for sufficient ridge regularization λ > λ c \lambda>\lambda_{c} , ensuring that the per-step contraction beats the noise injected by replacing μ 0 k \mu_{0}^{k} with μ ^ 0 k \widehat{\mu}_{0}^{\,k} . Comparison with prior work. The result extends the uniform-in-time backward propagation of chaos of [ 43 ] along two structural axes: depth , through a stack of attention layers with parameters shared across tokens, and measure interaction , through a contextual measure transported by the dynamics. The technical crux is the Lipschitz dependence of δ ​ ℒ / δ ​ θ \delta\mathcal{L}/\delta\theta on the contextual measure (Section 4 ), which transfers forward concentration into training stability.

The proof of Theorem 2.2 hinges on a precise analytical handle on the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameter path θ 	heta . The covector p s p_{s} runs backward in depth and tracks the sensitivity of the terminal loss to the position of the distinguished token at depth s s ; it is a direct generalization of the classical adjoint variable in the neural-ODE literature [ 22 ] . The scalar field ϕ s \phi_{s} plays the analogous role for the contextual measure: it tracks the sensitivity of the loss to perturbations of μ s \mu_{s} at depth s s , and its evolution couples back to the token adjoint through the source term involving δ ​ 𝒱 / δ ​ μ \delta\mathcal{V}/\delta\mu . sections.heading: Derivation in one sentence.
sections.text: The adjoint system ( 3.2 )–( 3.3 ) arises by introducing a Lagrangian for the constrained optimization problem of minimizing ℒ \mathcal{L} subject to ( 1.1 ), with p s p_{s} enforcing the token equation and ϕ s \phi_{s} enforcing the continuity equation, and then choosing the multipliers so that the variations of the Lagrangian with respect to x s x_{s} and μ s \mu_{s} vanish. The full computation, including the integration-by-parts manipulations that produce the cross terms in ( 3.3 ) and the well-posedness analysis of ( 3.3 ) via a contraction argument in a weighted C 1 C^{1} space, is given in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Relation to control theory.
sections.text: Adjoint systems featuring a Wasserstein-derivative term are well-known in the Pontryagin theory of McKean–Vlasov control [ 14 , 15 , 6 ] and in the optimal control of continuity equations [ 8 ] . The structure of ( 3.2 )–( 3.3 ) is closest in spirit to the major–minor mean-field formalism [ 45 , 16 ] , in which a distinguished agent interacts with a continuum population. Our contribution is not only the specific adjoint equation for contextual flow maps but also the stability estimates of Section 4 which are absent from the control literature.

sections.heading: Riemannian extension.
sections.text: The Eulerian Lagrange-multiplier argument is geometrically transparent and extends without modification to settings where the contextual flow is constrained to a Riemannian submanifold 𝐌 ⊆ ℝ d \mathbf{M}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} —for example, the unit sphere 𝕊 d − 1 \mathbb{S}^{d-1} relevant to post-LayerNorm transformers as in [ 38 ] . In that case p s p_{s} becomes a tangent vector in T x s ​ 𝐌 T_{x_{s}}\mathbf{M} , the spatial Jacobian D x ​ 𝒱 D_{x}\mathcal{V} is replaced by the covariant derivative ∇ 𝐌 𝒱 \nabla^{\mathbf{M}}\mathcal{V} , and ( 3.2 ) is modified accordingly.

sections.heading: 4. Stability estimates
sections.text: The forward and backward propagation-of-chaos bounds of Section 2 ultimately reduce to a number of stability estimates : quantitative statements asserting that the contextual flow ( 1.1 ), the adjoint system ( 3.2 )–( 3.3 ), and the loss gradient ( 3.1 ) all depend Lipschitz-continuously on their inputs, with constants that are uniform in depth. We collect the two estimates that drive the analysis in this section, and outline how they imply the main theorems. Full proofs are deferred to Appendices A and B .

sections.heading: 4.1. Stability of the contextual flow
sections.text: Let ( x s , μ s ) (x_{s},\mu_{s}) and ( x ~ s , μ ~ s ) (\widetilde{x}_{s},\widetilde{\mu}_{s}) denote the solutions of ( 1.1 ) associated with two parameter paths θ , θ ~ \theta,\widetilde{\theta} and two initial conditions ( x 0 , μ 0 ) (x_{0},\mu_{0}) and ( x ~ 0 , μ ~ 0 ) (\widetilde{x}_{0},\widetilde{\mu}_{0}) in ℝ d × 𝒫 ⁡ ( ℝ d ) \mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) , respectively. There exists C = C ⁡ ( 𝐀 ) C=C(\mathbf{A}) such that, for every s ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] s\in[0,1] , (4.1) W 1 ​ ( μ s , μ ~ s ) ≤ C ⁡ ( W 1 ​ ( μ 0 , μ ~ 0 ) + ‖ θ − θ ~ ‖ L 1 ) , \mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu_{s},\widetilde{\mu}_{s})\;\leq\;C\bigl(\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu_{0},\widetilde{\mu}_{0})\,+\,\|\theta-\widetilde{\theta}\|_{L^{1}}\bigr), (4.2) | x s − x ~ s | ≤ C ⁡ ( W 1 ​ ( μ 0 , μ ~ 0 ) + | x 0 − x ~ 0 | + ‖ θ − θ ~ ‖ L 1 ) . |x_{s}-\widetilde{x}_{s}|\;\leq\;C\bigl(\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu_{0},\widetilde{\mu}_{0})\,+\,|x_{0}-\widetilde{x}_{0}|\,+\,\|\theta-\widetilde{\theta}\|_{L^{1}}\bigr). sections.heading: 4.3. Stability estimates for transformers
sections.text: All the estimates above are stated under the abstract regularity assumptions collected in Assumption 5.1 on the velocity field 𝒱 \mathcal{V} . In Appendix E , we verify that the concrete self-attention vector field ( 1.2 ), together with standard MLP layers, satisfies these assumptions. Crucially, all resulting Lipschitz constants (and higher-order regularity constants) are independent of the embedding dimension d d and the parameter dimension p p —i.e., they are truly dimension-free. Our analysis builds upon prior work on the smoothness of attention. For example, [ 18 , 34 ] established Lipschitz continuity of the attention mechanism with respect to the input tokens (corresponding to D x ​ 𝒱 D_{x}\mathcal{V} and ∇ ∇ μ 𝒱 \nabla\mkern-10.0mu\nabla_{\mu}\mathcal{V} in our setting). In addition, we establish full Lipschitz continuity (together with the necessary higher-order regularity) with respect to both the tokens and the trainable parameter matrices Q , K , V Q,K,V themselves. Combined with the dimension-free nature of our constants, all the rates stated in Theorem 2.1 and Theorem 2.2 hold for realistic Transformer architectures with absolute constants; the only unavoidable dependence is on the input-support radius R R and the parameter-path bound M M .

sections.heading: Remark on localization.
sections.text: It suffices for Assumptions ( A3 )–( A4 ) and Assumption 5.2 to hold on the compact sets furnished by ( A1 ): our proofs invoke 𝒱 \mathcal{V} and its derivatives only along the trajectories of the contextual flow ( 1.1 ) and along the OGD iterates ( 2.3 ). We establish the requisite uniform-in-depth boundedness of both in Lemma C.1 and in Theorem A.1 below. In particular, when 𝒱 \mathcal{V} is a transformer block (a self-attention layer or an MLP), Assumptions ( A3 )–( A4 ) and Assumption 5.2 are derived from the single global hypothesis ( A1 ) with constants that are dimension-free (Appendix E ).

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced contextual flow maps as a unifying abstraction for analyzing transformers and developed a quantitative statistical theory in which the context length n n is the central statistical resource. Within this framework, we established forward and backward propagation-of-chaos bounds at the Wasserstein rate n − 1 / d n^{-1/d} , uniformly along the depth of the network and, in the regularized regime, uniformly along the iterates of online gradient descent. To our knowledge, these are the first such guarantees for a deep stack of attention layers, where tokens lose their initial independence after the first layer through the shared velocity field. Under the additional structural condition that contextual measure μ \mu is applied linearly when computing the vector field 𝒱 \mathcal{V} —a condition satisfied by self-attention—we sharpen these bounds to the parametric rate n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} , both for the distinguished token and along the OGD trajectory. Identifying weaker structural conditions under which the parametric rate persists is a natural direction for future work. A central technical ingredient, of independent interest, is the Eulerian adjoint equation of Section 3 . In contrast to the classical neural-ODE adjoint, which features a single covector for the distinguished token, the contextual setting requires two coupled adjoint variables: a covector p s p_{s} tracking sensitivity to the token, and a scalar test field ϕ s \phi_{s} tracking sensitivity to the contextual measure. The C 1 , 1 C^{1,1} -regularity of ϕ s \phi_{s} is exactly what allows Wasserstein stability of the loss gradient, and we expect this two-variable construction to be useful for stability analysis of trained transformers and for the Riemannian extension to post-LayerNorm architectures.

sections.heading: Appendix C Non-asymptotic OGD analysis: proof of Theorem 2.2
sections.text: This appendix proves Theorem 2.2 under Assumption 5.1 via three intermediate results: a uniform-in-iteration boundedness lemma for the OGD trajectory, a deterministic stability bound with respect to data and initialization, and a McDiarmid-type concentration bound for the empirical OGD trajectory.

sections.heading: Appendix E Verification of Assumption 5.1 and 5.2 for transformer architectures
sections.text: This appendix verifies that the standard transformer building blocks—self-attention layers ( 1.2 ) and MLP layers—satisfy Assumptions ( A3 ), ( A4 ), and ( 5.2 ), with constants that depend only on the support radius R R in ( A1 ), the parameter bound M M , and (for MLPs) the activation regularity. In particular all constants are independent of the embedding dimension d d and of the parameter dimension p p .

sections.heading: E.1. Self-attention blocks

sections.heading: Conclusion.
sections.text: Combining Propositions E.2 – E.5 for self-attention layers and Propositions E.10 – E.12 for MLP layers, every transformer block satisfies Assumptions ( A3 ) and ( A4 ) on the compact sets supplied by ( A1 ) (after Propositions E.1 and E.9 ), with constants depending only on ( M , R ) (M,R) and on the activation regularity α \alpha , and in particular independent of the embedding dimension d d and the parameter dimension p p . All results in Section 2 therefore apply to standard transformer architectures with absolute constants.

We develop a quantitative statistical theory of transformers in the large-context regime by adopting the abstraction of contextual flow maps (CFMs): dynamical systems that evolve a distinguished token in the presence of a contextual measure across a stack of attention blocks. Within this framework, the finite-context model approximates an idealized infinite-context system in which the contextual measure is replaced by its underlying population, so that the context length n n becomes a statistical resource. Exploiting the McKean–Vlasov structure of the dynamics and the classical machinery of propagation of chaos, we establish a forward bound controlling the deviation between the finite- and infinite-context CFMs uniformly along depth, and a backward bound controlling the deviation between the corresponding training trajectories uniformly across iterations of online gradient descent. Both bounds achieve the optimal Wasserstein rate n − 1 / d n^{-1/d} for general CFMs and parametric rate n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} for a restricted class of CFMs that includes transformers as a special case. The analysis rests on a new Eulerian adjoint formulation of the loss gradient and stability estimates for the resulting forward–adjoint system, both of which may be of independent interest. 1. Introduction The transformer architecture, introduced by Vaswani et al. [ 59 ] , is the foundation of modern machine learning systems, from large language models [ 29 ] to Vision Transformers [ 30 ] . A convenient way to view inputs to these models is through a distinguished token x ∈ ℝ d x\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that is updated in the presence of a context of n n tokens z ( 1 ) , … , z ( n ) ∈ ℝ d z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(n)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} encoded by the contextual measure μ = 1 n ​ ∑ i δ z ( i ) \mu= rac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\delta_{z^{(i)}} . In encoder-style models, x x is typically a prepended special token such as [CLS] ; in decoder-style models, it is the current final token whose representation is used to predict the next one. After passing through a deep stack of attention blocks, the model returns an output token y y whose value depends on both x x and its context. We refer to such maps as contextual maps . This viewpoint on transformers was developed in [ 33 ] , where transformers were shown to have universal approximation properties within the class of contextual maps. At the same time, the compositional structure of transformers, like that of deep neural networks more broadly, can be interpreted as a dynamical system, with the network realizing an input-to-output flow map [ 31 , 44 , 22 ] . Combining these perspectives suggests a natural abstraction: transformers as contextual flow maps , namely dynamical systems that evolve an input token-context pair ( x 0 , μ 0 ) (x_{0},\mu_{0}) across layers and produce an output token x 1 x_{1} . Three formalizations of transformers. The contextual measure μ 0 = 1 n ​ ∑ i δ z ( i ) \mu_{0}= rac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\delta_{z^{(i)}} can be regarded as an n n -sample empirical estimator of an underlying population measure μ 0 ∞ \mu_{0}^{\infty} . The contextual flow map ( 1.1 ) then takes this empirical measure as input and produces an output x 1 x_{1} that approximates an idealized infinite-context system, obtained by replacing μ 0 \mu_{0} with μ 0 ∞ \mu_{0}^{\infty} in ( 1.1 ). The infinite-context system is a natural reference because an ideal transformer should be able to operate on arbitrarily long context: as the context grows, the contextual measure μ 0 \mu_{0} resolves the underlying population μ 0 ∞ \mu_{0}^{\infty} ever more faithfully, and a model that fully exploits its context should reflect this in its output. The infinite-context system is exactly the object that does so, and the finite-context model should be understood as approximating it. From this perspective, the context length n n plays the role of a statistical resource: it is the budget the model is given to estimate the population on which the ideal transformer would act. We are thus led to the central question of the paper: How accurately does a finite-context contextual flow map approximate its infinite-context limit, as a function of the context length n n , both at inference time (forward pass) and during training (backward pass)? This question is of practical as well as theoretical interest: although recent advances have substantially extended the usable context window of large language models [ 56 ] , long contexts remain constrained by computational costs, which in turn limit the emergence of new capabilities. Quantifying the dependence on n n therefore informs how aggressively context can be reduced without compromising fidelity to the infinite-context reference. The McKean–Vlasov structure of ( 1.1 ) makes it tractable through the classical machinery of propagation of chaos [ 46 , 55 , 20 , 21 ] . Related work. The input-output behavior of transformers can be formalized in at least three ways: as a sequence-to-sequence map, a measure-to-measure map, and a contextual map; see Figure 1 . The sequence-to-sequence viewpoint models a transformer T : ( ℝ d ) n → ( ℝ d ) n T:(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}	o(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n} as a map from n n input tokens ( x 1 , … , x n ) (x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) to n n output tokens ( y 1 , … , y n ) (y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}) . This early and direct formalization was used to establish approximation results in [ 64 , 1 ] , albeit with architectures whose size grows exponentially in n n . Although this dependence can be alleviated by allowing the embedding dimension to scale with n n , the resulting growth in complexity remains restrictive in modern large-context applications. Early measure-theoretic foundations for attention were developed in [ 60 ] , which interpreted self-attention as a system of self-interacting particles and established regularity properties such as Lipschitz continuity under suitable assumptions. This line of work was substantially extended in the seminal paper [ 54 ] , where transformers were analyzed as a mean-field interacting particle system implementing a measure-to-measure map. This perspective has enabled the use of powerful tools from partial differential equations and Wasserstein gradient flows; see [ 37 , 36 , 13 , 12 , 23 , 17 , 53 , 11 , 24 , 39 , 3 , 2 ] . From a statistical viewpoint, a closely related recent contribution is [ 47 ] , which studies transformers as measure-theoretic associative memory and establishes generalization guarantees together with a matching minimax lower bound under spectral assumptions. Despite its usefulness, however, the measure-to-measure viewpoint does not explicitly capture the central role of the distinguished token. This limitation is addressed by the contextual-map formulation introduced in the [ 33 ] , which established universal approximation within the class of contextual flow maps using architectures whose size is independent of the context length. The relevance of this contextual framework extends well beyond approximation theory. It provides a natural language for the rapidly growing literature on in-context learning with transformers [ 10 , 63 , 35 , 4 , 61 , 26 , 5 ] . Moreover, it captures the structure of settings in which transformers are explicitly deployed as contextual velocity fields , notably in diffusion models [ 51 ] and measure-to-measure regression [ 58 ] . The present work adopts the same contextual viewpoint, but focuses on statistical questions rather than expressivity alone. The statistical behavior of transformers as the context length grows has received relatively little attention. Recent works [ 9 , 7 ] study the convergence of a single attention head applied to n n i.i.d. tokens to its infinite-token limit. While both establish a parametric n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} rate of convergence, the latter draws a more subtle picture near the hardmax limit. Our contribution differs in two major ways. First, we study a deep stack of attention layers using contextual flow maps rather than a single attention layer. In a deep stack the context tokens interact through the shared velocity field 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , so they lose their initial independence after the first layer; bounding the deviation from the infinite-context limit therefore requires tracking the growth of correlations across layers. Second, we also study the generalization of training dynamics from finite to infinite context length. Our analysis is accordingly closer in spirit to the theory of propagation of chaos for McKean–Vlasov dynamics. We emphasize that in our setting the term refers to quantitative mean-field stability bounds rather than the convergence of finite marginals to product measures as in [ 49 ] . Nevertheless, we adopt it as it has become standard in the machine learning literature [ 27 , 50 , 41 , 42 , 40 , 28 , 19 ] . While our work does not require the full apparatus of the theory, we borrow its key structural insight: controlling deviations through regularity of the velocity fields, in both the forward and the backward pass. Uniform-in-time propagation of chaos for the backward pass of two-layer feedforward networks—simple maps f θ : ℝ d → ℝ d f_{	heta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}	o\mathbb{R}^{d} —was recently established in [ 43 ] . We extend these results to contextual flow maps, which (i) account for depth and (ii) depend on an evolving measure. Our contributions. We initiate a quantitative statistical theory of contextual flow maps in the large-context regime, treating the context length n n as the central statistical resource. Under mild regularity assumptions on the velocity field 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , our main results are the following. (C1) Forward propagation of chaos. We establish a quantitative deviation bound between the finite-context contextual flow map ( 1.1 ) and its infinite-context limit, holding uniformly along the depth of the network (Theorem 2.1 ). The analysis explicitly tracks the propagation of correlations introduced at each layer by the shared velocity field—a mechanism that is absent from the single-layer analyses of [ 9 , 7 ] . (C2) Backward propagation of chaos. We obtain a deviation bound between the Online Gradient Descent (OGD) training trajectory of a finite-context model and that of its infinite-context counterpart, holding uniformly over all iterations of the algorithm (Theorem 2.2 ). This extends the recent two-layer feedforward result of [ 43 ] along two structural axes: (i) depth, through a stack of attention layers with parameters shared across tokens, and (ii) interaction with an evolving contextual measure that is itself transported across layers. (C3) Adjoint equation for contextual flows. We derive an Eulerian adjoint formulation of the loss gradient (Theorem 3.1 in Section 3 ) that couples a covector adjoint for the distinguished token to a scalar adjoint test function for the contextual measure. This formulation underlies all of our stability analysis and extends naturally to the Riemannian setting relevant to post-LayerNorm transformers. (C4) Stability estimates. Our results rest on a new set of stability estimates for the contextual flow and the loss gradient (Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 in Section 4 ), established uniformly in depth and uniformly along the parameter path. We further show in Section 4.3 that the standard transformer architecture—both self-attention and MLP layers—satisfies these estimates with Lipschitz constants that are independent of the embedding dimension and parameter count , suggesting a structural reason why transformers train stably across model scales. Assumptions. Our results rest on two sets of assumptions, stated as Assumptions 5.1 and 5.2 . The first is purely technical: routine regularity conditions (compactness, smoothness of the various objects entering the definition of CFMs) of the kind required by any analysis of this type. Some can likely be relaxed, but regularity of some form is unavoidable. The second assumption plays a more substantive role. It is not needed to establish our slow rates n − 1 / d n^{-1/d} ; rather, it is the precise structural ingredient that upgrades these to the parametric rate n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} . The adjoint system ( 3.2 )–( 3.3 ) arises by introducing a Lagrangian for the constrained optimization problem of minimizing ℒ \mathcal{L} subject to ( 1.1 ), with p s p_{s} enforcing the token equation and ϕ s \phi_{s} enforcing the continuity equation, and then choosing the multipliers so that the variations of the Lagrangian with respect to x s x_{s} and μ s \mu_{s} vanish. The full computation, including the integration-by-parts manipulations that produce the cross terms in ( 3.3 ) and the well-posedness analysis of ( 3.3 ) via a contraction argument in a weighted C 1 C^{1} space, is given in Appendix B . Relation to control theory. Adjoint systems featuring a Wasserstein-derivative term are well-known in the Pontryagin theory of McKean–Vlasov control [ 14 , 15 , 6 ] and in the optimal control of continuity equations [ 8 ] . The structure of ( 3.2 )–( 3.3 ) is closest in spirit to the major–minor mean-field formalism [ 45 , 16 ] , in which a distinguished agent interacts with a continuum population. Our contribution is not only the specific adjoint equation for contextual flow maps but also the stability estimates of Section 4 which are absent from the control literature. Riemannian extension.
